title: How to Pick the Perfect Breathable Kurta for Summer's Worst Heat
excerpt: From cotton and mulmul to linen and chanderi, a practical guide to staying cool and stylish when the mercury climbs.
body:
• Cotton, mulmul, and linen are the top three breathable fabrics for summer kurtas, each with distinct advantages depending on the occasion.
  • Mulmul (fine muslin) is the lightest option, absorbing moisture while feeling almost weightless on the skin.
  • Linen kurtas look sharp but wrinkle quickly — best reserved for relaxed outings, not all-day wear.
  • Chanderi cotton offers a subtle sheen for festive occasions while remaining comfortable in the heat.

When summer temperatures in India cross 40°C and humidity makes stepping outside feel like walking into a steam room, the kurta remains one of the few garments that manages to be both stylish and genuinely comfortable. But not all kurtas are created equal — and the fabric you choose can mean the difference between surviving the day and wilting before noon.

Cotton: The Reliable All-Rounder

Pure cotton remains the gold standard for summer kurtas, and for good reason. The fabric absorbs sweat, allows air to circulate freely, and feels soft from the first wear. For everyday use — commuting, office wear, running errands — a well-cut cotton kurta in a neutral shade is hard to beat.

The key is picking the right weave. Lightweight, matte cotton works best; avoid thick or stiff varieties that trap heat. Block-printed cotton kurtas from Jaipur, in pastel blues, sage greens, and off-whites, have become wardrobe staples precisely because they combine comfort with visual interest. Brands across India now offer cotton kurta sets ranging from ₹2,000 for everyday wear to ₹15,000 and above for designer labels like Ranna Gill and Esha Arora.

"Cotton is breathable, lightweight, and comfortable, making it perfect for hot climates."

— The Loom, Summer Collection 2026

Mulmul: The Ultra-Light Secret Weapon

If cotton is the workhorse, mulmul — also known as fine muslin — is the sports car. This ultra-light fabric has been woven in India for centuries, and for peak summer heat, nothing comes close. Mulmul kurtas feel like a second skin, allow maximum airflow, and dry quickly after absorbing perspiration.

The fabric drapes beautifully, making it a favourite for flowy Anarkali-style kurtas. For diaspora members visiting India during summer, a mulmul kurta set is arguably the most practical ethnic wear investment. The only downside: mulmul is delicate and requires gentle washing, so it is better suited for occasions than daily rough use.

Linen: Style-First, Comfort-Second

Linen kurtas have surged in popularity, driven by their crisp, structured look and Instagram-friendly aesthetic. The fabric absorbs up to 20 percent of its weight in moisture before feeling damp and dries faster than cotton, according to fabric experts. It also feels three to four degrees cooler against the skin than synthetic alternatives.

But linen has a well-known weakness: wrinkles. Within hours of wearing, a linen kurta develops visible creases, which limits its appeal for formal settings or long workdays. Linen works best for weekend brunches, resort holidays, and photo-friendly outings where the slightly rumpled look reads as intentional rather than dishevelled.

Chanderi: Understated Elegance

For festive occasions that still demand comfort — temple visits, small gatherings, casual celebrations — chanderi cotton strikes the right balance. This handwoven fabric from Madhya Pradesh combines a subtle sheen with genuine breathability, making it feel dressier than plain cotton without the discomfort of silk or polyester.

Chanderi kurtas pair well with delicate dupattas and minimal jewellery, creating a polished look that does not require sacrificing comfort. They tend to be pricier than standard cotton, but a single chanderi set can anchor a summer wardrobe for years.

What to Avoid

Synthetic blends — polyester, rayon, and viscose — should be avoided in peak summer. These fabrics trap heat, feel sticky against the skin, and can cause irritation during long wear. Heavy embroidery and dense linings also add unnecessary weight and insulation. The rule is simple: the lighter the fabric and the looser the fit, the cooler you stay.

For those building a summer capsule wardrobe, fashion experts recommend six to eight kurtas in breathable fabrics, two neutral-tone bottoms, and two lightweight dupattas. That combination yields 15 to 20 outfit variations — more than enough for a full Indian summer.
